observed: Title identifies poteto, also Lauren Tan, working on Grok Bot. The title's 'except mine' joke sets up skepticism about how we judge other people's code.
mechanism: She proposes earning trust through the engineering environment. Branding and agent preference do not establish quality.
apply: Judge our generated changes by observable behavior, constraints, and maintenance cost.

observed: 'Our blessed craft / their barbarous slop' labels equivalent agents, prompting, iteration, and 4,000-line PRs differently.
mechanism: This exposes inconsistent standards. A familiar author or preferred model can make the same engineering practice seem acceptable.
apply: Use the same acceptance criteria for human and agent changes. A large PR needs evidence regardless of author.

observed: Her personal chart shows March–October PR counts: 68, 254, 352, 685, 1,113, 2,401, 2,932, 3,127; total 10,932.
mechanism: She attributes scaling to roughly six months improving the environment. The count is an output measure; the chart does not reveal PR size, task value, or cost.
apply: Treat this as motivation for reducing repeated supervision. Track useful completed work and escaped defects alongside throughput.

observed: 'Quality & quantity' and 'everyone can be a coding machine.' Her thesis is increasing output while maintaining or improving quality.
mechanism: Agents lower the cost of producing code; engineering effort shifts toward making that output reliable.
apply: Define what quality means for each product before increasing autonomous work: correctness, responsiveness, accessibility, recovery, and operability.

observed: A conceptual curve plots trust against the number of agents, from one through thousands. It is an illustration, without measured trust units.
mechanism: More parallel work is manageable only when each change requires less scarce human attention.
apply: Increase concurrency after measuring reliable unattended completion. Do not interpret the curve as evidence that running more agents creates trust.

observed: The low-trust loop is 'agent writes slop code → human verifies it → issues found.' The human remains the bottleneck.
mechanism: Repeated verbal corrections solve individual instances while leaving the next instance equally likely.
apply: Record recurring review findings and convert suitable ones into APIs, type constraints, lint rules, or behavioral tests.

observed: The high-trust build adds 'agent writes good code → agent verifies it → issues found.' It still contains feedback and failure detection.
mechanism: Verification becomes part of the agent's normal task, with tools capable of revealing mistakes before handoff.
apply: Require the agent to run the relevant checks and exercise the real user journey, then deliver the evidence with the change.

observed: The inverted poteto pyramid lists codebase; static analysis; verification; prose; human review. A downward arrow is labeled cost. The slide groups tests and CI under 'static analysis,' although many tests execute code.
mechanism: Spend heavily on reusable constraints and preserve expensive judgment for what those layers cannot settle. She highlights each layer in successive builds.
apply: Prioritize clear APIs and architecture, machine-enforced checks, runtime/formal verification, concise judgment guidance, then targeted human review. The drawing is a prioritization model, not quantified cost accounting.

observed: 'Code is memory' overlays the pyramid. She says the codebase is one of an agent's largest inputs.
mechanism: Repository patterns teach future implementations. An enforced improvement persists across tasks more reliably than an isolated correction in chat.
apply: Replace deprecated examples and make the preferred implementation easy to discover. Repository cleanup improves the context supplied to the next agent.

observed: A building covered in vegetation illustrates code arriving as a continuous, almost organic stream.
mechanism: The building's structure shapes where growth can occur. Architecture plays that role for rapidly generated code.
apply: Create explicit boundaries and reusable primitives before scaling generation. Folder naming alone is insufficient without checks.

observed: The same building gains the label 'Organic Architecture.' She describes constraints as foundations around which new code grows.
mechanism: Architecture is maintained continuously as patterns appear, rather than treated as a one-time diagram.
apply: Use recurring agent mistakes as feedback about the shape of our abstractions and module boundaries.

observed: 'Each copy makes the next copy more likely' shows one workaround propagating through connected weeds into 'the pattern.'
mechanism: Agents may infer that repeated code is the accepted local convention. Duplication gives a bad technique apparent legitimacy.
apply: Prevent new instances first, then migrate existing ones so agents cannot keep learning from them. Link the replacement API in the diagnostic.

observed: 'Yes, you should read the code sometimes' appears beside a human asking the agent to walk through it.
mechanism: The talk retains an explicit role for understanding implementation, despite later claims about reduced deep review of routine product code.
apply: Read framework changes, critical invariants, and unfamiliar algorithms. Use walkthroughs to expose assumptions, then encode what can be checked.

observed: Dune combines an app framework for navigation, rendering, and IPC with one folder per feature, strict import bans, and no comments in code. She describes it as roughly Next.js for Electron.
mechanism: A narrow paved path packages expertise into framework behavior and lint constraints. Product work uses that path repeatedly.
apply: Build a thin product foundation around our chosen platform. Dune's internal implementation is not supplied by this talk; pstack is a separate public skill collection.

observed: 'Nuance tends to lead to slop — just design better APIs.' She says useEffect is banned in product code and allowed only in selected Dune internals.
mechanism: Move difficult lifecycle decisions into a small framework layer instead of expecting every agent to use a subtle primitive correctly.
apply: Provide approved APIs for subscriptions, data loading, timers, and cleanup before restricting direct primitives. Scope restrictions to the layer where an alternative exists.

observed: electron-renderer contains features, client, primitives; electron-main contains startup, notifications, update. Direct imports are crossed out with 'not even types'; both depend on shared types in shared/. A side-project file src/sim/tick.hot.ts signals 'runs every tick' and 'no allocations.'
mechanism: Names convey execution context, and dependency analysis/linting enforces it. Shared contracts avoid importing implementation across process boundaries.
apply: Use equivalent UI/domain/platform boundaries on mobile and desktop. For Electron, preserve typed IPC through an appropriate bridge. Do not interpret the import ban as a ban on legitimate process communication.

observed: 'Stop agents from writing unsolicited markdown.' The illustration says 'Source?' and 'I made it up.' She describes agents turning corrections into excessive hard rules or documenting excuses.
mechanism: Unreviewed prose can create fictional requirements and rationalize architectural shortcuts.
apply: Keep maintained specifications and feature maps with owners; prevent incidental task notes from silently becoming policy. This requested analysis is intentional documentation, not the behavior she criticizes.

observed: The timer example progresses Sep 9 → Oct 3 → Oct 17: setTimeout(() => release(id), 0), justified as fixing flicker, is copied into a shared module and becomes '183 timers.'
mechanism: She connects timer proliferation to a mismatch between VS Code's imperative architecture and React's declarative model, plus allocation/GC overhead. A zero-delay timer postpones work; it does not establish correct ownership or ordering.
apply: Repair lifecycle, cancellation, and resource ownership. Ban unsupported scheduling shortcuts in product layers and provide a supported primitive. The slide's 'it would be a larger change' excuse is not a correctness argument.

observed: 'Comments are liabilities' shows 65,824 on July 31 and 1,227 'today,' referencing /no-comments. She says they banned roughly 99% because comments stale and cannot enforce behavior.
mechanism: A comment can preserve a plausible explanation while the implementation remains wrong. Fewer comments is her team's policy, not an experimentally established cause of fewer bugs.
apply: Prefer explicit APIs and executable rules. Preserve necessary rationale, external contracts, legal text, and assumptions that cannot be expressed usefully in code; choose our policy deliberately.

observed: 'Whenever you correct your agent' shows an increasing staircase labeled 7, 17, 38, 90, 139, 149, 157, 167. The caption says 'lint against it or categorically eliminate the problem.' The y-axis does not specify a unit.
mechanism: Corrections accumulate into durable constraints instead of repeated supervision. She explicitly recommends better API design or architecture when a lint is not enough.
apply: For each repeated issue, ask whether it is syntactically detectable, expressible in types, behaviorally testable, or requires an architectural change. Avoid inventing a rule for a one-off preference.

observed: 'Verification is the most important step' overlays the pyramid. She says review now focuses on videos, screenshots, diagrams, and formal verification.
mechanism: A verification artifact lets reviewers inspect a claim about behavior without deriving the entire behavior from a diff.
apply: Attach relevant evidence to the exact build or commit. A screenshot is evidence of visible state; persistence, side effects, and timing need additional observations.

observed: The feature map has three explicit columns: what features exist, how users reach it, what proves it works. The slide references /create-verification-skill.
mechanism: It gives users and agents a shared vocabulary and tells the agent both how to exercise a feature and how to recognize success.
apply: Map the first few important journeys with prerequisites, visible entry points, actions, expected state, side effects, and evidence. Keep the map synchronized with the product.

observed: A CLI is added: app aria-click --accessible-name "Settings"; app snapshot; app screenshot proof.png. Labels say 'drive the real app' and 'agent checks its own work.'
mechanism: Reusable, testable commands replace freshly improvised automation scripts and reduce token use. Stable accessibility names form part of the control surface.
apply: Expose launch, readiness, interaction, snapshots, screenshots/recording, logs, and cleanup through one maintained driver. These are slide examples; no installed executable named app is established.

observed: TLA+ is presented for modeling state machines and checking rules; Lean for proofs about algorithms. She cites notification flows across devices and a custom virtualizer's flicker/jitter behavior, and calls the approach promising but experimental.
mechanism: Model checking explores reachable behavior in a specified model; proof checking validates a formal claim under assumptions. They target different failure classes.
apply: Model cancellation, retries, sync, and notification acknowledgement; prove selected indexing or layout algorithms when worthwhile. Track how the model/proof corresponds to actual code. The talk does not supply the models, proofs, bounds, or implementation-linkage details.

observed: An embedded video demonstrates UI property-based testing with github.com/antithesishq/bombadil. It opens menus, settings, bot creation, and other states while entering unusual strings.
mechanism: Generate many action/input sequences and check invariants, reaching combinations that a scripted happy path misses. She reports finding UI bugs; the clip does not reveal its property definitions or seeds.
apply: Define invariants such as no crash, no cross-account state, recoverable navigation, and no duplicate send. Save seed, action trace, build, and failure artifact so findings become reproducible regressions. Native UI needs a compatible driver rather than assuming this browser-oriented library covers every platform.

observed: A May 15, 2026 Cindy Sridharan post says subtle bugs in AI-generated PRs required several additional days and substantial manual verification.
mechanism: Code generation speed can hide downstream repair work. Reviewing only initial output time understates total cost.
apply: Measure time to verified completion and follow-up fixes, not just initial PR creation.

observed: A Nov 5, 2026 follow-up says 70% of daily token spend verifies patches and about 20–30% creates them. Lauren says most of her own usage similarly goes to verification.
mechanism: Lower-cost generation makes extensive checking economical. The quoted percentage is one practitioner's reported allocation, not a controlled optimum.
apply: Budget verification explicitly and measure value per check. Allocate depth according to risk rather than imposing a universal 70% quota.

observed: A lifecycle chart spans pre-production, deploy, release, post-release: unit/functional/component/fuzz/property/formal/static/mutation/coverage/benchmark/contract/lint/acceptance/regression/smoke/usability/UI/penetration/threat/performance work; integration/tap-compare/load/shadowing/config/soak; canarying/monitoring/traffic-shaping/feature flags/exception tracking; teeing/profiling/logs/chaos/monitoring/A-B/tracing/dynamic exploration/real-user monitoring/auditing/on-call.
mechanism: Verification continues after code tests pass and after deployment. She argues agents reduce the cost of applying established engineering methods.
apply: Choose coverage by failure mode and lifecycle stage. The chart is a menu of techniques, not proof her team runs every technique for every PR.

observed: /statechart links to pstack and shows a large user-flow diagram with highlighted problem paths.
mechanism: A user-oriented state machine makes requirements and counterexample paths reviewable alongside runtime video and screenshots.
apply: Review the agreed states and invariants before relying on an agent's implementation. A Mermaid diagram by itself does not establish that a model checker ran or that implementation conforms.

observed: 'Ok so what' transitions from methods to results.
mechanism: The next charts are evidence she offers for the approach. They are a team's observational results, without a controlled comparison.
apply: Assess the complete group of metrics rather than treating PR volume as sufficient evidence.

observed: Team merged PRs June–October: 809, 1,984, 4,203, 5,648, 10,926; total 23,570. The spoken '11,000' is rounded.
mechanism: A rising number of contributors and changes accompanies the tooling investment. The chart does not isolate effects of staffing, PR sizing, model changes, or task mix.
apply: Track throughput, change size, rework, quality, compute cost, and delivered outcomes together. Do not make raw PR count a target.

observed: Desktop releases: August since launch 7, September 19, October 15; total 41. Median time between releases: 44, 25, 28 hours.
mechanism: She describes this as roughly daily stable releases. A 28-hour median interval is not equivalent to releasing on every calendar day.
apply: Distinguish merge, deploy, staged rollout, stable release, and actual adoption. Mobile store review and binary distribution impose different release constraints.

observed: Contributors June–October: 15, 48, 95, 163, 227. October bins: 49 with one PR, 78 with 2–9, 77 with 10–99, 22 with 100–999, one with 1,000+.
mechanism: The environment supports both core contributors and low-context drive-by work. Growth in people also contributes to growth in total PRs.
apply: Test whether a fresh contributor or agent can launch, find a feature, make a constrained change, and verify it without tribal knowledge.

observed: Revert rate is labeled '% of commits reverted': June 0.98%, July 0.61%, August 0.47%, September 0.48%, October 0.47%.
mechanism: The relative revert measure falls while volume grows. It excludes defects corrected forward, undetected problems, and other outcomes unless they lead to counted reverts.
apply: Preserve the denominator. Pair it with incidents, escaped defects, forward-fix/rework, customer impact, and recovery time. Avoid calling 0.47% the overall bug rate.

observed: May→now: cold launch 2,304→1,395ms; relaunch 1,348→829ms; first paint 2,268→1,379ms; short-chat median typing 3.8→2.8ms; long-chat median 8.4→2.9ms and p90 9.7→3.4ms; settings 112→92ms; long-chat cold open 153→165ms, warm 138→86ms; switch to short chat 88→49ms, back to long 105→63ms; resize 3.0→6.9ms; idle memory 488→545MiB; idle CPU 0.40→0.80%; startup JS+CSS 2.0→7.7MB.
mechanism: Most shown interaction latencies improve, but five measurements regress: cold long-chat open, resize, memory, idle CPU, and startup assets. Hardware, workload, repetitions, and benchmark method are not given.
apply: Keep performance budgets across responsiveness, resource use, startup, and package size. The slide supports mixed improvement, not universal improvement. Rust is mentioned only as a possible rewrite idea.

observed: The full pyramid returns at the conclusion.
mechanism: Architecture, automated checks, verification, concise prose, and judgment are prerequisites to scaling automation.
apply: Start with our recurring failure classes and cheapest durable prevention. Tool installation alone will not create the environment she describes.

observed: 'Should I build a software factory?' clarifies that this means automating writing, shipping, and deploying code.
mechanism: The factory is a layer built on a reliable development loop.
apply: Identify which parts of our loop already produce verifiable outcomes before introducing scheduled or event-triggered work.

observed: 'Don't automate a bad loop' compares low and high trust with the caption 'improve your loop before automating.'
mechanism: Automating a failure-prone process increases the rate and cost of producing defects and repair work.
apply: Make a single agent's reproduce→fix→verify cycle dependable first. Add external triggers once that cycle works on representative tasks.

observed: The animation adds a third loop labeled factory with an automated trigger. It still contains writing, verification, and feedback.
mechanism: Automation supplies work and repeats a proven loop; it does not replace checking.
apply: Give automated jobs explicit scope, completion evidence, resource limits, and failure handling. These implementation controls are our proposed design, not configuration shown in the talk.

observed: Grok Bot outer-loop inputs include feedback on X, a Linear ticket, a new Slack message, cron/schedule, and Datadog/Sentry alerts. A shared team bot feeds an inner coding/verification loop. Link: x.ai/bot.
mechanism: Connectors and routines initiate coding agents and projects. The outer loop decides when work starts; the inner loop produces and checks changes.
apply: Separate trigger ingestion/triage from execution, verification, and merge policy. Use our available orchestrator; the concept does not depend on Grok Bot or Cursor.

observed: The displayed Linux x64 .deb fuzz report compares a stable build with 0.79.4 and checks published SHA-256 values. It uses a local backend from main and a saved copy of production gate values. After merging two duplicate pairs: 50 distinct bugs, three new (0 high/two medium/one low), 47 existing (one high/nine medium/37 low); the high issue also exists in 0.79.4. Findings are separate replies, new first then severity.
mechanism: This is artifact-level, baseline-aware exploration with environment disclosure and deduplication. The narration says releases trigger fuzzing, fix PRs, and auto-merge; the screenshot itself is a findings report and does not show those fixes passing or merging.
apply: Verify the actual packaged build, record provenance and flags, compare against a baseline, preserve replayable evidence, deduplicate, then create fixes that rerun checks. Implement platform-specific release validation and choose merge gates according to risk.

observed: The closing title changes to 'all code is slop (except yours).' She returns to high velocity with quality through foundations.
mechanism: Trust is supported by the surrounding system rather than an assertion that generated code is inherently reliable.
apply: Our reusable asset should be a maintained engineering environment: product framework, constraints, feature map, driver, verification, evidence, and feedback.
